Relations and Functions32 questions

Q1CUET 2026 · 20 May, Shift 1 · Q26worked here
Let R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2)} be a relation on {1, 2, 3}. The minimum number of elements to be added so that R is an equivalence relation is:
  1. 4
  2. 3
  3. 5
  4. 1
Concept to recallAdd only what each property forces: symmetric partners, then transitive closures.
  1. Reflexive already. Symmetry forces (2, 1).
  2. {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)} is transitive (the class {1, 2} plus {3}).
  3. So 1 element.

Answer: option (4) — 1

NoteThe source prints “(1)”, which is ambiguous between the value 1 and the first option (4); the value is 1.
Q2CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q321NTA final key
Relation R in the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, …, 16} defined as R = {(x, y) : 3x = y, x, y ∈ A}, then which of the following are correct?
A. domain of R = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
B. range of R = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15}.
C. R is reflexive.
D. R is not symmetric.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A and B only
  2. B and D only
  3. A, B and C only
  4. A, B and D only
Concept to recallList the pairs; domain = first entries, range = second entries.
  1. R = {(1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12), (5, 15)} (3 × 6 = 18 > 16).
  2. Domain {1, …, 5}, range {3, 6, 9, 12, 15}: A, B true.
  3. (1, 1) ∉ R: not reflexive. (1, 3) ∈ R but (3, 1) ∉ R: not symmetric (D true).

Answer: option (4) — A, B and D only

Q3CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q322NTA final key
A function f : N → N, (N : set of natural numbers) defined by f(x) = x2 + x + 1 is
  1. one-one and onto
  2. one-one but not onto
  3. many-one and onto
  4. many-one but not onto
Concept to recallStrictly increasing on N ⇒ one-one; check whether small values are hit.
  1. For x ≥ 1, f is strictly increasing (f′ = 2x + 1 > 0), so one-one.
  2. Least value f(1) = 3, so 1 and 2 have no pre-image: not onto.

Answer: option (2) — one-one but not onto

Q4CUET 2026 · 15 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q1key re-derived
Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 4, 6}. A function f : A → B is defined by f(x) = 2x. The function is:
  1. One-one only
  2. Onto only
  3. Both one-one and onto
  4. Neither one-one nor onto
Concept to recallOne-one: distinct inputs, distinct outputs. Onto: range = codomain.
  1. f(1) = 2, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 6: all different, so one-one.
  2. Range {2, 4, 6} = B, so onto: f is a bijection.

Answer: option (3) — Both one-one and onto

Q5CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q2key re-derived
If R = {(x, y) | x, y ∈ ℤ, x2 + y2 ≤ 4} is a relation in ℤ, then the domain of R is:
  1. {0, 1, 2}
  2. {0, −1, −2}
  3. {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}
  4. {−1, 0, 2}
Concept to recallDomain of R = set of first entries of its pairs.
  1. x2 ≤ 4 − y2 ≤ 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}.
  2. Each such x pairs with y = 0, so all five occur.

Answer: option (3) — {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}

Q6CUET 2026 · 18 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q3key re-derived
If R = {(x, y) | x, y ∈ ℝ, x2 + y2 = 1} is a relation in ℝ, then R is:
  1. Reflexive
  2. Symmetric
  3. Transitive
  4. Equivalence Relation
Concept to recallTest each property with a counterexample; swapping x and y leaves x² + y² unchanged.
  1. Symmetric: x2 + y2 = y2 + x2.
  2. Not reflexive: (2, 2) ∉ R since 8 ≠ 1.
  3. Not transitive: (1, 0), (0, 1) ∈ R but (1, 1) ∉ R.

Answer: option (2) — Symmetric

Q7CUET 2026 · 21 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q7key re-derived
Let R be defined on ℕ by (a, b) ∈ R if and only if a + b is even. R is:
  1. Equivalence Relation
  2. Symmetric but not Transitive Relation
  3. Reflexive but not Symmetric Relation
  4. Anti-symmetric Relation
Concept to recalla + b even ⇔ a and b have the same parity.
  1. a + a = 2a is even: reflexive. a + b = b + a: symmetric.
  2. a, b same parity and b, c same parity ⇒ a, c same parity: transitive.

Answer: option (1) — Equivalence Relation

Q8CUET 2026 · 22 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q10key re-derived
Find the number of relations on a set A with exactly 3 elements.
  1. 9
  2. 64
  3. 512
  4. 27
Concept to recallA relation on A is any subset of A × A; |A × A| = n2, so there are 2n² relations.
  1. |A × A| = 9, so 29 = 512 relations.

Answer: option (3) — 512

Q9CUET 2026 · 29 May, Shift 1 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q9key re-derived
Let R be a relation on {1, 2, 3} defined by R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2)}. Identify the properties satisfied by R.
  1. Symmetric only
  2. Reflexive and Transitive
  3. Equivalence relation
  4. None of these
Concept to recallCheck each property on the listed pairs.
  1. All (a, a) present: reflexive.
  2. (1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R: not symmetric.
  3. The only chains are through (a, a), which add nothing new: transitive.

Answer: option (2) — Reflexive and Transitive

Q10CUET 2026 · 31 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q7key re-derived
The number of relations on A = {1, 2, 3} containing at most 6 elements including (1, 2), that are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, is:
  1. 4
  2. 5
  3. 6
  4. 7
Concept to recallReflexive forces the 3 pairs (a, a); with (1, 2) that is 4 pairs, leaving at most 2 more.
  1. Base {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2)}: reflexive, transitive, not symmetric (1 relation).
  2. Add one more pair: (1,3) and (3,2) keep it transitive; (2,1) makes it symmetric; (2,3) needs (1,3) and (3,1) needs (3,2), so they fail alone. 2 relations.
  3. Add two pairs: {(1,3), (2,3)}, {(1,3), (3,2)}, {(3,1), (3,2)} are transitive and not symmetric; every other pair of pairs breaks transitivity. 3 relations.
  4. Total 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

Answer: option (3) — 6

NoteThis 31 May S2 set reads like JEE Main problems rather than CUET ones; it is kept as the site gives it, with the answer checked here.
Q11CUET 2025 · 14 May, Shift 1 · Q66NTA final key
Let f: R → R be defined as f(x) = 10x. Then (Where R is the set of real numbers)
  1. f is both one-one and onto
  2. f is onto but not one-one
  3. f is one-one but not onto
  4. f is neither one-one nor onto
Concept to recallOne-one: f(x1) = f(x2) ⇒ x1 = x2. Onto: every y in the codomain has a pre-image.
  1. 10x1 = 10x2 ⇒ x1 = x2: one-one.
  2. For any real y, x = y/10 is real and f(x) = y: onto.

Answer: option (1) — f is both one-one and onto

TrapOn N or Z, 10x would not be onto; on R it is.
Q12CUET 2025 · 14 May, Shift 1 · Q67NTA final key
Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Then, the number of relations containing (1, 2) and (1, 3), which are reflexive and symmetric but not transitive, is
  1. 1
  2. 2
  3. 3
  4. 4
Concept to recallBuild the smallest relation with the required properties, then check what can be added without breaking them.
  1. Reflexive + symmetric + containing (1, 2), (1, 3) forces R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1), (1,3), (3,1)}.
  2. R is not transitive: (2,1), (1,3) ∈ R but (2,3) ∉ R.
  3. The only pairs left are (2,3), (3,2); symmetry forces both together, and then R = A × A, which is transitive.
  4. So exactly one such relation.

Answer: option (1) — 1

Q13CUET 2024 · 16 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q23NTA final key
If the function f : ℕ → ℕ is defined as f(n) = {n − 1,if n is evenn + 1,if n is odd, then
(A) f is injective   (B) f is into   (C) f is surjective   (D) f is invertible
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
  1. (B) only
  2. (A), (B) and (D) only
  3. (A) and (C) only
  4. (A), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallA bijection is one-one and onto, and exactly the bijections are invertible.
  1. f swaps 1 ↔ 2, 3 ↔ 4, 5 ↔ 6, …; f(f(n)) = n.
  2. So f is its own inverse: one-one, onto, invertible. It is not into.
  3. Correct: (A), (C), (D).

Answer: option (4) — (A), (C) and (D) only

Q14CUET 2024 · 16 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q45NTA final key
Let R be the relation over the set A of all straight lines in a plane such that l1 R l2 ⇔ l1 is parallel to l2. Then R is :
  1. Symmetric
  2. An Equivalence relation
  3. Transitive
  4. Reflexive
Concept to recallNCERT convention: every line is taken as parallel to itself, so "is parallel to" is an equivalence relation.
  1. Reflexive (l ∥ l), symmetric, transitive ⇒ equivalence relation.
  2. Options (1), (3), (4) are each true but incomplete; the most appropriate is (2).

Answer: option (2) — An Equivalence relation

Q15CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q566NTA final key
Relation R on the set A = {1, 2, 3, …, 13, 14} defined as R = {(x, y) : 3x − y = 0} is :
  1. Reflexive, symmetric and transitive
  2. Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
  3. Neither reflexive nor symmetric but transitive
  4. Neither reflexive nor symmetric nor transitive
Concept to recallList the pairs, then test each property with a counter-example.
  1. R = {(1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12)}.
  2. (1, 1) ∉ R: not reflexive. (3, 1) ∉ R: not symmetric.
  3. (1, 3), (3, 9) ∈ R but (1, 9) ∉ R: not transitive.

Answer: option (4) — Neither reflexive nor symmetric nor transitive

Q16CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q573NTA final key
Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined as f(x) = 10 − x2, then :
  1. f is one-one and onto.
  2. f is one-one but not onto.
  3. f is neither one-one nor onto.
  4. f is onto but not one-one.
Concept to recallOne-one fails if two inputs share an output; onto fails if some codomain value is never reached.
  1. f(1) = f(−1) = 9: not one-one.
  2. Range is (−∞, 10]; 11 is never reached: not onto.

Answer: option (3) — f is neither one-one nor onto.

Q17CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q401NTA final key
Let f(x) = |x| and g(x) = [x], then the value of fog(−92) − gof(−92) is :
  1. −1
  2. 1
  3. −9
  4. 9
Concept to recall[x] is the greatest integer ≤ x: [−4.5] = −5, not −4.
  1. fog(−4.5) = |[−4.5]| = |−5| = 5.
  2. gof(−4.5) = [4.5] = 4.
  3. Difference = 1.

Answer: option (2) — 1

TrapTaking [−4.5] = −4 makes both 4 and the answer 0.
Q18CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q402NTA final key
Let R be a relation on the set of integers Z such that R = {(a, b), a = 2kb, a, b, k ∈ Z}, then R is :
  1. Reflexive but not Symmetric and Transitive
  2. Symmetric and Reflexive but not Transitive
  3. Equivalence relation
  4. Reflexive and Transitive but not Symmetric
Concept to recallCheck each property with the exponent k: k = 0 (reflexive), −k (symmetric), k1 + k2 (transitive).
  1. a = 20a: reflexive.
  2. a = 2kb ⇒ b = 2−ka, and −k ∈ Z: symmetric.
  3. a = 2kb, b = 2mc ⇒ a = 2k+mc: transitive.
  4. So R is an equivalence relation.

Answer: option (3) — Equivalence relation

TrapBecause k may be negative, symmetry holds; with k ≥ 0 only it would fail.
Q19CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q431 also CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q96 (same function, options worded ‘one-one / onto’ and reordered; NTA key: ‘neither one-one nor onto’)NTA final key
The function f : R → R, f(x) = x2 is :
  1. injective but not surjective
  2. surjective but not injective
  3. injective as well as surjective
  4. neither injective nor surjective
Concept to recallOne-one: f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b. Onto: range = codomain.
  1. f(−1) = f(1): not injective.
  2. Negative reals have no pre-image: not surjective.

Answer: option (4) — neither injective nor surjective

Q20CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q66NTA final key
For real numbers a and b, define aRb if b − a + √5 is an irrational number. Then the relation R is:
  1. Symmetric
  2. Reflexive
  3. Transitive
  4. Equivalence
Concept to recallTest each property; one counterexample kills symmetry or transitivity.
  1. a − a + √5 = √5 is irrational: reflexive.
  2. a = 0, b = √5: b − a + √5 = 2√5 (0R√5), but a − b + √5 = 0 is rational: not symmetric.
  3. a = 1, b = √5, c = 1 − √5: aRb (2√5 − 1) and bRc (1 − √5), both irrational; but c − a + √5 = 0 is rational: not transitive.
  4. So R is reflexive only.

Answer: option (2) — Reflexive

Q21CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q67NTA final key
The domain of the function f(x) = log(x2 − 4) is :
  1. [2, ∞)
  2. (−∞, −2) ∪ (2, ∞)
  3. (2, ∞)
  4. (−∞, −2] ∪ (−2, −1)
Concept to recalllog u needs u > 0 (strictly).
  1. x2 − 4 > 0 ⇒ |x| > 2.
  2. Domain (−∞, −2) ∪ (2, ∞).

Answer: option (2) — (−∞, −2) ∪ (2, ∞)

Trap[2, ∞) includes 2 (log 0 is undefined) and misses the negative branch.
Q22CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q901NTA final key
If f(x) = ex and g(x) = logex = lnx, then (gof)(x) is
  1. e
  2. x
  3. e2x
  4. loge2x
Concept to recall(g o f)(x) = g(f(x)); ln and ex are inverse functions.
  1. g(f(x)) = ln(ex) = x.

Answer: option (2) — x

Q23CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q902NTA final key
The region R on the set A = {x ∈ Z : 0 ≤ x ≤ 12}, given by R = {(a, b) : |a − b| is a multiple of 4} is :
  1. Reflexive but not Symmetric
  2. Reflexive but not Transitive
  3. Symmetric but not Transitive
  4. Equivalence relation
Concept to recall“a − b divisible by n” (congruence mod n) is always an equivalence relation.
  1. Reflexive: |a − a| = 0 = 4 · 0.
  2. Symmetric: |a − b| = |b − a|.
  3. Transitive: a − b = 4m, b − c = 4n ⇒ a − c = 4(m + n).
  4. Hence an equivalence relation.

Answer: option (4) — Equivalence relation

Note“The region R” is as printed; read it as “the relation R”.
Q24CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q851NTA final key
The relation R in the set A = {1, 2, 3, 4} is given by R = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (1, 1), (4, 4), (1, 3), (3, 3), (3, 2)} is:
  1. Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
  2. Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
  3. Symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
  4. an equivalence relation
Concept to recallCheck each property against the listed pairs; for transitivity check every chain (a, b), (b, c).
  1. Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) all present.
  2. Not symmetric: (1, 2) ∈ R but (2, 1) ∉ R.
  3. Transitive: the only chains with distinct steps are (1,3),(3,2) → (1,2) ∈ R; every other chain passes through a loop (a, a).

Answer: option (2) — Reflexive and transitive but not symmetric

Q25CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q852NTA final key
If f(x) = 27x3 and g(x) = (x)1/3, then gof(x) is:
  1. x
  2. 2x
  3. 3x
  4. 0
Concept to recallgof(x) = g(f(x)).
  1. g(27x3) = (27x3)1/3 = 3x.

Answer: option (3) — 3x

Q26CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q881NTA final key
Set A has 4 elements and the set B has 6 elements, then the number of injective mappings that can be defined from A to B is :
  1. 360
  2. 15
  3. 24
  4. 1296
Concept to recallOne-one maps from an m-set to an n-set (m ≤ n): nPm = n!/(n − m)!.
  1. 6P4 = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360.

Answer: option (1) — 360

Trap1296 = 64 counts all functions; 15 = 6C4 forgets the order of assignment.
Q27CUET 2023 · date unknown (partial paper) · Q66worked here
Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Consider the relation R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 3)}. Then R is
  1. reflexive only
  2. reflexive and transitive
  3. symmetric and transitive
  4. neither symmetric nor transitive
Concept to recallReflexive: every (a, a). Symmetric: (a, b) ⇒ (b, a). Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ⇒ (a, c).
  1. (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) present: reflexive.
  2. (1, 2) but no (2, 1): not symmetric.
  3. The only chain of distinct pairs is (1, 2), (2, 3), and (1, 3) is present: transitive.

Answer: option (2) — reflexive and transitive

NoteNo answer key exists for this paper; the answer is worked here.
Q28CUET 2023 · date unknown (partial paper) · Q67worked here
If f : R → R is defined by f(x) = sin x + x, then f(f(x)) is:
  1. 2 sin x + 2x
  2. sin2x + x2
  3. sin(sin x + x) + sin x + x
  4. sin2x + 2 sin x + x
Concept to recallf(f(x)): replace every x in f(t) = sin t + t by t = f(x).
  1. f(t) = sin t + t with t = sin x + x.
  2. = sin(sin x + x) + sin x + x.

Q29CUET 2023 · date unknown (partial paper) · Q96worked here
The range of the function f(x) = 13 − sin 4x is:
  1. [14, 12]
  2. [12, 1]
  3. [14, 34]
  4. [12, 34]
Concept to recallBound the denominator first, then take reciprocals (which reverses the inequalities for positive numbers).
  1. −1 ≤ sin 4x ≤ 1 ⇒ 2 ≤ 3 − sin 4x ≤ 4.
  2. 1/4 ≤ f(x) ≤ 1/2.

Q30CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q16key re-derived
Which of the following is not an equivalence relation on Z?
  1. a R b ⇔ a + b is an even integer
  2. a R b ⇔ a − b is an even integer
  3. a R b ⇔ a ≤ b
  4. a R b ⇔ a = b
Concept to recallEquivalence = reflexive, symmetric and transitive. ≤ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric.
  1. (1) a + b even ⇔ same parity: an equivalence. (2) and (4) are equivalences.
  2. (3): 1 ≤ 2 but 2 ≤ 1 is false — not symmetric.

Answer: option (3) — a R b ⇔ a ≤ b

Q31CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q17key re-derived
The function f : R − {−1} → R − {1} defined by f(x) = xx + 1 is
  1. Both 1-1 and onto
  2. Only 1-1
  3. Only onto
  4. Neither 1-1 nor onto
Concept to recallOne-one: f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b. Onto: solve y = f(x) for x and check x lies in the domain for every y in the codomain.
  1. a/(a + 1) = b/(b + 1) ⇒ a = b: one-one.
  2. y = x/(x + 1) ⇒ x = y/(1 − y), defined for every y ≠ 1 and never equal to −1: onto.

Answer: option (1) — Both 1-1 and onto

Concept to recallFor t > 0, cot−1 t = tan−1(1/t); tan−1 is one-one.

  3. t = 2 + √3 > 1 gives x > 0; t = 2 − √3 < 1 gives x < 0.

Answer: option (2) — There is one positive and one negative real value of x satisfying the above equation.

  4. 23(cot(x23 − 1) − x cosec2(x23 − 1))
Concept to recalld(log sin u)/du = cot u; d(cot u)/du = −cosec2u. Product rule for the second derivative.
  1. u = x2/3 − 1, u′ = 2x/3. y′ = (2x/3) cot u.
  2. y″ = (2/3) cot u + (2x/3)(−cosec2u)(2x/3) = (2/3) cot u − (4x2/9) cosec2u.

Answer: option (2) — 23 cot(x23 − 1) − 4x29 cosec2(x23 − 1)

Q262CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q27key re-derived

Q263CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q28key re-derived

Concept to recallSquare and factor first: the relation reduces to y = −x/(1 + x), so dy/dx = −1/(1 + x)2.
  1. x2(1 + y) = y2(1 + x) ⇒ (x − y)(x + y + xy) = 0; x ≠ y ⇒ y = −x/(1 + x).
  2. At x = −3: y = 3/(−2) = −3/2, y′ = −1/4.
  3. 2y′ + y = −1/2 − 3/2 = −2.

Q265CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q4worked here

Q270CUET 2026 · 20 May, Shift 1 · Q10key re-derived
For the function f(x) = ax + bx, a > 0, b > 0, which of the following statements are correct?

  2. f(0) = 2, f(1) = 0, f(2) = 8 − 6 + 2 = 4.
  3. Absolute maximum = 4.

Answer: option (1) — 4

TrapStopping at the critical point gives 0, which is the minimum.

Q299CUET 2024 · 16 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q13NTA final key

Q302CUET 2024 · 16 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q34NTA final key
f(x) = sin x + 12 cos 2x in [0, π2]

Q303CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q555NTA final key

Q304CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q557NTA final key

Q308CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q392NTA final key

  1. (0, 1)

Concept to recall|x − a| is a V with vertex at x = a: decreasing to the left, increasing to the right.
  1. For x > 1, f(x) = x − 1, f′ = 1 > 0.
  2. For x < 1, f′ = −1: decreasing. So increasing on (1, ∞).

Answer: option (4) — (1, ∞)

Q309CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q414NTA final key
For which values of a, f(x) = a(x + sin x) is an increasing function ?

  2. a ∈ (0, ∞)

Concept to recallNCERT calls f increasing on I when x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) ≤ f(x2), i.e. f′ ≥ 0 on I; strictly increasing needs <.
  1. f′(x) = a(1 + cos x), and 1 + cos x ≥ 0 for every x.
  2. So f′ ≥ 0 everywhere exactly when a ≥ 0; for a < 0 the function decreases.
  3. a = 0 gives the constant function, which is increasing in NCERT’s (non-strict) sense, so a ∈ [0, ∞).

Answer: option (3) — a ∈ [0, ∞)

TrapDropping a = 0 answers ‘strictly increasing’, not ‘increasing’: NTA’s final key is (3), [0, ∞).
Q310CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q415NTA final key

  1. f′(x) = sec2x − 1 = tan2x > 0 on (0, π/2).
  2. So f is increasing.

Answer: option (1) — increasing function

Q311CUET 2023 · 17 Jun, Shift 3 · Q416NTA final key

Q315CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q79NTA final key

Q318CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q891NTA final key

  1. dy/dx = 1 + cos 2x; at x = −π/2, cos(−π) = −1, so dy/dx = 0.

Q319CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q892NTA final key
A particle is moving along the curve y = 34x4 + 3. The point on the curve at which y-coordinate is changing thrice as fast as the x coordinate, is :
  1. (1, −9/4)
  2. (0, 3)
  3. (1, 15/4)
  4. (−1, 15/4)
Concept to recallRates along a curve: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).
  1. dy/dt = 3x3 dx/dt. Require dy/dt = 3 dx/dt, so x3 = 1, x = 1.
  2. y = 3/4 + 3 = 15/4. Point (1, 15/4).

Trap(−1, 15/4) is on the curve but there x3 = −1, so y changes 3 times as fast in the opposite direction.
Q320CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q914NTA final key
The tangent to the curve x = cos t(3 − 2cos2t), y = sin t(3 − 2sin2t) at t = π4, makes with the x-axis an angle :
  1. 0
  2. π4
  3. π6
  4. π3
Concept to recallSlope of a parametric curve = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); the angle with the x-axis is tan−1(slope).
  1. x = 3cos t − 2cos3t: dx/dt = −3sin t + 6cos2t sin t = 3 sin t cos 2t.
  2. y = 3sin t − 2sin3t: dy/dt = 3cos t − 6sin2t cos t = 3 cos t cos 2t.
  3. dy/dx = cos t / sin t = cot t; at t = π/4, slope = 1, angle = π/4.

Answer: option (2) — π4

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus. Strictly, both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish at t = π/4 (cos 2t = 0), so the slope is taken as the limit cot t → 1 after cancelling cos 2t — the intended (and keyed) reading.
Q321CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q915NTA final key

  4. strictly increasing in (5π/4, 2π]

Q324CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q864NTA final key
The slope of the normal to the curve y = 2x2 + 3sinx at x = 0, is:

  2. −3

Q325CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q865NTA final key
If the function f(x) = k sinx + 2 cosxsinx + cosx is increasing for all values of x, then
  1. k < 1
  2. 1 < k
  3. k > 2
  4. k < 2
Concept to recallQuotient rule; f increasing ⇔ f′ > 0.
  1. Numerator of f′: (k cosx − 2 sinx)(sinx + cosx) − (k sinx + 2 cosx)(cosx − sinx).
  2. The sin·cos terms cancel, leaving k(cos2 + sin2) − 2(sin2 + cos2) = k − 2.
  3. f′ = (k − 2)/(sinx + cosx)2 > 0 ⇒ k > 2.

Answer: option (3) — k > 2

Q326CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q866NTA final key

  1. 1000 cm2
  2. 225 cm2
  3. 625 cm2
  4. 500 cm2

  1. rθ = 100 − 2r, so A = ½r(100 − 2r) = 50r − r2.
  2. dA/dr = 50 − 2r = 0 ⇒ r = 25 (d2A/dr2 = −2 < 0, a maximum).
  3. A = 50(25) − 625 = 625 cm2.

Answer: option (3) — 625 cm2

Q327CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q882NTA final key

  2. Maximum value 2.

Trap3 is where the maximum occurs, not its value.
Q328CUET 2023 · date unknown (partial paper) · Q73worked here
A manufacturer can sell x items at a price of ₹3x + 5 each. The cost price of x items is ₹x2 + 5x. If x is the number of items she should sell to get no profit and no loss, then:

Q336CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q43key re-derived
Passage. Case Study: An online retail company ships its product in cartons. Each carton is made by rectangular sheet of fiber board with dimension of 8 m by 3 m.   2. 23
  3. 1

Concept to recallCritical points from f′ = 0; keep only those inside the physical range 0 < x < 3/2; confirm with f″ < 0.
  1. 12x2 − 44x + 24 = 4(3x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 ⇒ x = 2/3 or 3.
  2. x = 3 is impossible (the 3 m side would be negative).
  3. f″(x) = 24x − 44; f″(2/3) = −28 < 0: maximum at x = 2/3.

Answer: option (2) — 23

  1. f(0) = 0 ⇒ B = −A; f′(0) = 2A = 3 ⇒ f(x) = 32(ex − e−x).
  2. f(ln 3) = 32(3 − 13) = 4.
  3. 9 × 4 = 36.

Answer: option (3) — 36

Q478CUET 2026 · 31 May, Shift 2 · memory-based (findmycollege) · Q5key re-derived
Let y = y(x) satisfy cos x (log cos x)2 dy + (sin x − 3y sin x log cos x) dx = 0, x ∈ (0, π/2). If y(π/4) = −1log 2, then y(π/6) equals:
  1. 1log 3 − log 4
  2. 1log 2
  3. 1log 3
  4. 1log 4
Concept to recallSubstitute t = log cos x (dt = −tan x dx) to turn it into a linear DE in t.
  1. Dividing by cos x · t2 and using dt/dx = −tan x: dy/dt + 3y/t = 1/t2.
  2. I.F. t3: y t3 = t2/2 + C.
  3. At π/4, t = −½ log 2, y = −1/log 2: y t3 = (log 2)2/8 = t2/2, so C = 0 and y = 1/(2t).
  4. At π/6, 2t = log(3/4): y = 1/(log 3 − log 4).

Answer: option (1) — 1log 3 − log 4

Q479CUET 2025 · 14 May, Shift 1 · Q61NTA final key
Which of the following are linear first order differential equations?
  1. (A) dydx + P(x)y = Q(x)
  2. (B) dxdy + P(y)x = Q(y)
  3. (C) (x − y)dydx = x + 2y
  4. (D) (1 + x2)dydx + 2xy = 2
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. (A), (B) and (D) only
  2. (A) and (B) only
  3. (A), (B) and (C) only
  4. (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Concept to recallLinear in y: y and y′ appear only to the first power and are never multiplied together (coefficients may depend on x).
  1. (A) is the standard form in y; (B) is the standard form with x as the dependent variable.
  2. (C): y·y′ appears (and as dy/dx = (x + 2y)/(x − y) it is homogeneous), so not linear.
  3. (D): divide by 1 + x2: y′ + [2x/(1 + x2)]y = 2/(1 + x2), linear.

Answer: option (1) — (A), (B) and (D) only

Q480CUET 2025 · 14 May, Shift 1 · Q62NTA final key

  2. 3e3x + 4e−4y + C = 0, where C is constant of integration
  3. 4e−3x + 3e4y + C = 0, where C is constant of integration
  4. 3e−3x + 4e4y + C = 0, where C is constant of integration

  2. Integrate: −e−4y/4 = e3x/3 + k.
  3. Multiply by −12: 3e−4y + 4e3x + C = 0.

Answer: option (1) — 4e3x + 3e−4y + C = 0, where C is constant of integration

TrapOption 2 swaps the 3 and 4 coefficients: the coefficient of e3x comes from the 1/3, so after clearing it is 4.

  1. Divide by x ln x: y′ + y/(x ln x) = 2/x.
  2. ∫dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x), so IF = eln(ln x) = logex.

  4. (D) Its general solution is loge(xy) = Cy, where C is constant of integration
  5. (E) If y(1) = 1, then its particular solution is y = x
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

  2. (A) and (D) only
  3. (B) and (C) only
  4. (B), (C) and (E) only
Concept to recalldy/dx = F(y/x) is homogeneous: put y = vx.
  1. dy/dx = (y/x)[ln(y/x) + 1]: homogeneous (B), not linear (contains y ln y).
  2. y = vx: v + xv′ = v ln v + v ⇒ dv/(v ln v) = dx/x.
  3. ln(ln v) = ln x + ln C ⇒ ln(y/x) = Cx: (C) true, (D) false.
  4. y(1) = 1 ⇒ C = 0 ⇒ y/x = 1, y = x: (E) true.

Answer: option (4) — (B), (C) and (E) only

Answer: option (2) — A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

NoteStrictly, B as printed is already polynomial in dy/dx with power 1 (the fractional powers are on x and y, not on the derivative), so its degree is 1. The intended reading — squaring to clear the roots — gives (dy/dx)2 and “degree 2”. The other three pairs fix option (2) anyway, and NTA’s key is (2).

Q512CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q11key re-derived
The solution curve of the differential equation loge(dydx) = 3x + 4y, passing through the origin is

Q513CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q13key re-derived
The curve represented by the differential equation dydx = 2(x + 1)yx2 + 2x + 2, y > 0, passes through the point (0, 4). If it also passes through P(−1, k) and Q(λ, 10) then (PQ)2 is equal to
  1. 148
  2. 66
  3. 68
  4. 72
Concept to recallSeparate: dy/y = 2(x + 1)dx/(x2 + 2x + 2) — the numerator is the derivative of the denominator.
  1. log y = log(x2 + 2x + 2) + log C; (0, 4): C = 2. So y = 2(x2 + 2x + 2).
  2. k = 2(1 − 2 + 2) = 2.
  3. 10 = 2(λ2 + 2λ + 2) ⇒ λ2 + 2λ − 3 = 0 ⇒ λ = 1 or −3.
  4. P(−1, 2) is on the axis of symmetry x = −1, so both Q give PQ2 = 22 + 82 = 68.

Answer: option (3) — 68

Q515CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q11worked here
For differential equation yex/ydx = (xex/y + y2)dy, y(0) = 1, the value of x(e) is equal to :
  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 2
  4. e
Concept to recallSpot an exact differential: d(x/y) = (ydx − xdy)/y2, so d(ex/y) = ex/y(ydx − xdy)/y2.
  1. Rearrange: ex/y(ydx − xdy) = y2dy; divide by y2: d(ex/y) = dy.
  2. ex/y = y + C. At x = 0, y = 1: 1 = 1 + C, C = 0.
  3. So ex/y = y, i.e. x = y log y.
  4. At y = e: x = e · 1 = e.

Answer: option (4) — e

Note“x(e)” means the value of x when y = e; the solution is naturally x as a function of y.
Q516CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q61worked here

  4. 6

Q517CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q9worked here
If a and b are order and degree of differential equation y″ + (y′)2 + 2y = 0, then value of 2a + 6b, is :
  1. 3
  2. 4
  3. 6
  4. 10
Concept to recallOrder = highest derivative present; degree = power of that highest derivative once the equation is a polynomial in derivatives.
  1. Highest derivative y″: order a = 2.
  2. It appears to power 1: degree b = 1.
  3. 2a + 6b = 4 + 6 = 10.

Answer: option (4) — 10

TrapThe square on y′ does not set the degree; only the highest-order derivative counts.

Q551CUET 2023 · 20 Jun, Shift 3 · Q100NTA final key

Concept to recallCollinear (parallel) vectors: y = λx, i.e. their components are proportional; directions may be same or opposite, magnitudes anything.

E. Equation of plane with intercepts 2, 3 and 4 on x, y and z-axis respectively is 2x + 3y + 4z = 1.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A, E only
  2. A, C, D only
  3. C, D, E only
  4. E only
Concept to recallLine through (x1, y1, z1) along (a, b, c): (x − x1)/a = …; intercept form of a plane: x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.
  1. A: correct in intent (the third member should read (z − 3)/(−2); see note).
  2. B: (4 − y)/5 = (y − 4)/(−5), so the direction is (3, −5, 6), and the point gives z − 3: false.
  3. C: direction (5, −2, 3) through O: true.
  4. D: normal (2, 3, −1) through (1, 2, 3): true.
  5. E: the intercept form is x/2 + y/3 + z/4 = 1, not 2x + 3y + 4z = 1: false.
  6. Correct: A, C, D.

Answer: option (2) — A, C, D only

TrapReading (4 − y)/5 as direction +5 makes B look right.
NoteNo answer key exists for this paper. Statement A is printed with ‘y − 3’ in the third fraction, an evident misprint for z − 3; no option contains C and D without A, so the intended answer is A, C, D.

Q627CUET 2026 · 20 May, Shift 1 · Q33key re-derived

  1. 7

Q655CUET 2024 · 19 Jul (re-test, CBT) · Q590worked here
Minimise Z = −50x + 20y
subject to the constraints : 2x − y ≥ −5, 3x + y ≥ 3, 2x − 3y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

  4. (A), (C) and (D) only
Concept to recallUnbounded region: a corner value m is the minimum only if the open half plane Z < m has no point in common with the region.
  1. Corners: (0, 5), (0, 3), (1, 0), (6, 0); Z = 100, 60, −50, −300. The region is unbounded: (A) true.
  2. Test −50x + 20y < −300: the point (9, 2) is feasible and gives Z = −410. So −300 is not the minimum.
  3. Along 2x − 3y = 12, Z = −(110x + 240)/3 → −∞: Z has no minimum. (B) true; (C), (D) false.

No option is correct as printed — see the note.

NoteNTA dropped this question in the final key (every candidate got the marks). This is NCERT Ch. 12 Example 5, whose answer is "Z has no minimum value". Option (1) is the tempting one: it holds the true (A) but also the corner value −300 of (D), which is not a minimum.

  3. A, B and C only

Concept to recallBounded region ⇒ both optima exist at corners; unbounded ⇒ they may not exist. Optima can occur at two corners (and the edge between).
  1. A true (unbounded regions may lack an optimum).
  2. B false: the maximum can occur at two corners (a whole edge).
  3. C true: with x, y ≥ 0 and a, b > 0, Z ≥ 0 everywhere, and Z(0, 0) = 0.
  4. D false: on an unbounded region Z can grow without bound.
  5. So A and C only.

Answer: option (2) — A and C only

NoteThe Hindi version of this question asks which statements are not true; the English text, followed here and by NTA’s key, asks which are true.
Q671CUET 2023 · 2 Jul, Shift 3 · Q878NTA final key

Q674CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q15key re-derived
The corner points of the feasible region of an LPP are (0, 0), (30, 0), (20, 30) and (0, 50). If the objective function maximize (z) = ax + by, where a ≠ b and a, b > 0, has alternate optimal solutions, then

  2. a = 3b
  3. 2a = b
  4. 3a = b

Answer: option (2) — a = 3b

Q681CUET 2026 · 20 May, Shift 1 · Q44key re-derived

Q686CUET 2026 · 24 May, Shift 2 · Q354NTA final key
The probability of the simultaneous occurrence of two events A and B is p. If the probability that exactly one of A and B occurs is q, then
A. P(A̅) + P(B̅) = 2 + 2q − p
B. P(A̅) + P(B̅) = 2 − 2p − q
C. P(A̅ ∩ B̅) = 1 − p − q
D. P((A ∩ B)|(A ∪ B)) = pp + q
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. A, C and D only
  2. B, C and D only
  3. C and D only
  4. B only
Concept to recallExactly one: P(A) + P(B) − 2P(A ∩ B); P(A ∪ B) = exactly one + both.
  1. P(A) + P(B) = q + 2p ⇒ P(A̅) + P(B̅) = 2 − 2p − q (B true, A false).
  2. P(A ∪ B) = p + q ⇒ P(A̅ ∩ B̅) = 1 − p − q (C true).
  3. P(A ∩ B | A ∪ B) = p/(p + q) since A ∩ B ⊂ A ∪ B (D true).

Answer: option (2) — B, C and D only

  3. (A) – (III), (B) – (IV), (C) – (II), (D) – (I)
  4. (A) – (III), (B) – (II), (C) – (I), (D) – (IV)
Concept to recallP(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A); P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B); P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
  1. P(A ∩ B) = 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32 → (II).
  2. P(A|B) = 0.32/0.5 = 0.64 → (III).
  3. P(A ∪ B) = 0.8 + 0.5 − 0.32 = 0.98 → (IV).
  4. P(A') = 0.2 → (I).

Answer: option (2) — (A) – (II), (B) – (III), (C) – (IV), (D) – (I)

Q710CUET 2024 · 16 May (pen & paper) · Sets A–D · Set A Q42NTA final key
There are two bags. Bag-1 contains 4 white and 6 black balls and Bag-2 contains 5 white and 5 black balls.   1. 49
  2. 38
  3. 27
  4. 419
Concept to recallBayes' theorem: P(E1|A) = P(E1)P(A|E1) / Σ P(Ei)P(A|Ei).

  3. P(W) = (1/3)(4/10) + (2/3)(5/10) = 4/30 + 10/30 = 14/30.
  4. P(Bag-1 | W) = (4/30)/(14/30) = 2/7.

Q729CUET 2023 · 23 Jun, Shift 3 · Q929NTA final key

Q739CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q39worked here
A bag contains 5 red and 7 black balls. Three balls are chosen at random one by one without replacement. What is the probability that the third ball is a Red ball given that first ball is red and second ball is black?
  1. 733
  2. 1433
  3. 766
  4. 2033
Concept to recallConditional probability without replacement: after the given draws, count what is left in the bag.
  1. After one red and one black are drawn: 4 red, 6 black remain.
  2. P(third red | first red, second black) = 4/10 = 2/5.
  3. 2/5 is not among the options. The option 7/66 is P(red, black, red) = (5/12)(7/11)(4/10) = 140/1320 = 7/66, the joint probability of the three draws.

No option is correct as printed — see the note.

Trap“Given that” means the first two draws have already happened; do not multiply in their probabilities.
NoteNo option is correct as the question is worded: the conditional probability is 2/5. Aakash prints “Answer (*)” (no option). Option (3), 7/66, is clearly what the setter computed — the probability that the draws are red, black, red in that order. If the question had asked for that joint probability, (3) would be right.
Q740CUET 2022 · 8 Aug, Slot 1 · Q40key re-derived
If two independent events A and B are such that P(A) = 12 and P((A′ ∩ B′)′) = 35, then P(B) is equal to
  1. 110
  2. 15
  3. 25
  4. 35
Concept to recallDe Morgan: (A′ ∩ B′)′ = A ∪ B. Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
  1. P(A ∪ B) = 3/5 = 1/2 + p − p/2 ⇒ p/2 = 1/10 ⇒ p = 1/5.

Answer: option (2) — 15

Q741CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q13worked here

  1. 12
  2. 112
  3. 16
  4. 13
Concept to recallAddition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
  1. P(A ∩ B) = 5/12 + 3/12 − 7/12 = 1/12.

Answer: option (2) — 112

Q743CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q71worked here
If events A and B are independent, then identify the correct statements
  1. A and B must be mutually exclusive
  2. The sum of their probabilities must be equal to 1
  3. P(A)·P(B) = P(A ∩ B)
  4. A′ and B′ are also independent
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
  1. A and B only
  2. B and C only
  3. C and D only
  4. A and D only
Concept to recallIndependent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Then A′, B′ (and A, B′) are independent too. Independent events with non-zero probabilities can never be mutually exclusive.
  1. C is the definition: true.
  2. P(A′ ∩ B′) = 1 − P(A) − P(B) + P(A)P(B) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)): D true.
  3. A and B are false in general.

Answer: option (3) — C and D only

Trap“Independent” and “mutually exclusive” are different ideas; if P(A), P(B) > 0 they are incompatible.
Q744CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q73worked here

  1. 415
  2. 845
  3. 13
  4. 29
Concept to recallIf A, B are independent so are A′, B′: P(A′ ∩ B′) = P(A′)P(B′).
  1. P(A′) = 2/5, P(B′) = 5/9.
  2. Product = 10/45 = 2/9.

Answer: option (4) — 29

Q745CUET 2022 · 30 Aug, Shift 2 (Set 32) · Q75worked here
A biased dice is thrown once. If X denotes the number appearing on it and have probability distribution :
x123456
P(X = x)kk/22k8k21−5kk/2
where k > 0. Then consider the following statements :
  1. P(X = 3).
  2. P(X ≤ 2).
  3. P(X ≥ 5).
  4. P(X = 4).
  5. P(X = 1) + P(X = 5).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
  1. C>D>B>A>E
  2. E>C>D>A>B
  3. E>C>A>B>D
  4. C>E>A>B>D
Concept to recallThe probabilities of a distribution add to 1; that fixes k.
  1. k + k/2 + 2k + 8k2 + 1 − 5k + k/2 = 1 ⇒ 8k2 − k = 0 ⇒ k = 1/8 (k > 0).
  2. P(1..6) = 1/8, 1/16, 1/4, 1/8, 3/8, 1/16.
  3. A = 1/4 = 0.25; B = 3/16 ≈ 0.19; C = 3/8 + 1/16 = 7/16 ≈ 0.44; D = 1/8 = 0.125; E = 1/8 + 3/8 = 1/2.
  4. E > C > A > B > D.

Answer: option (3) — E>C>A>B>D

NoteNot in the CUET 2026 syllabus.
